title: How Close Are We To Fully Autonomous Chip Design?
gist: In a SEMICON West keynote interview, Synopsys CEO Sassine Ghazi says AI agents already take a customer spec to verified RTL autonomously, with physical implementation and sign-off still ahead and humans still needed for architecture and final sign-off. System companies are pushing EDA to shorten spec-to-tape-out below a year because AI models change every three to four months, while 3D-IC thermal and mechanical failures drive the multiphysics logic behind the Ansys acquisition.

insights.claim: Synopsys has moved from AI-assisted optimization (reinforcement learning introduced around 2016) to orchestrating more than 40 task agents that are experts in its tools, with long-horizon orchestration letting a user specify only an outcome.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Agent-based EDA is a product shift that could change Synopsys's value capture and pricing from per-tool to per-outcome.
insights.quote: Today, we've moved from an assistant to an actual orchestration of multiple task agents. We have more than 40 task agents.
insights.locator: Around the 2016 time frame, we introduced reinforcement learning

insights.claim: Synopsys says the recent leap came from advances in model intelligence and reasoning over the last year or so, allowing models to orchestrate multiple agents toward a stated outcome.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Better reasoning in frontier models directly expands what chip-design automation can do.
insights.locator: The magic that has happened over the last year or so

insights.claim: Synopsys already has customer engagements where its Autonomous Agent takes a system company's spec to verified RTL, a step that used to take many months for many human engineers.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Spec-to-RTL automation is live and compresses early design schedules for hyperscaler and AI-lab customers.
insights.locator: That's the ambition. Today, we do have a number of engagements

insights.claim: Autonomy in physical implementation, physical verification and chip sign-off is not available today, though the Synopsys CEO has no doubt the industry will get there.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: The remaining back-end steps are the next milestones to watch for fully autonomous design claims.
insights.quote: I have no doubt we'll get there. Is this here today? No.
insights.locator: That's the ambition

insights.claim: Synopsys argues autonomous orchestration is positive for the industry because the binding constraint is a shortage of human engineers able to architect silicon from a spec, while demand for customized silicon is massive; humans still define architecture and sign off before manufacturing.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Automation is framed as relieving a talent bottleneck and expanding custom-silicon starts rather than cutting EDA demand.
insights.locator: Now the question typically comes up then

insights.claim: The Synopsys CEO says the model is fantastic at reasoning and exploring but the tool, accessed through the agent, is still needed to generate and validate and to choose the one implementation with the best performance, power and cost.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: EDA tool vendors argue their validated tools remain the control point even as general models improve.
insights.locator: Maybe a different way to ask the question

insights.claim: AI models are changing every three to four months, so system companies are taking control of their silicon development and pushing for faster cycles than the two-to-three-year silicon update norm.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Faster design cycles favor EDA vendors with AI automation and reinforce custom-silicon programs at hyperscalers.
insights.quote: the model is changing every three to four months. You cannot have silicon being updated every two to three years.
insights.locator: And that's why you have every system company trying to take control

insights.claim: Semiconductor customers are pushing development cycles down from 18, 16 or 14 months toward a year, and system companies are asking Synopsys to cut spec-to-tape-out to under a year or even under nine months.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Sub-year tape-out targets raise demand for EDA automation and put pressure on any step that cannot be accelerated.
insights.locator: And many of our semiconductor customers are pushing

insights.claim: System companies prioritize speed of spec definition and customization over programmability of chiplets or whole chips, and expect customized silicon to have a lifecycle of only two to three years rather than multiple model generations.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Demand favors fast turnover of workload-specific chips over adaptable hardware, a point against reconfigurable-silicon theses.
insights.quote: I'm not seeing it adopted too much by system companies
insights.locator: Yes, the whole programmability of either a chiplet

insights.claim: EDA R&D intensity as a percentage of revenue has always been high and Synopsys has not seen AI let that investment fall; its investment continues to increase.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: AI productivity gains are not translating into lower R&D spending, which matters for EDA margin expectations.
insights.quote: the investment that we're making is actually continuing to increase, not decrease
insights.locator: As a percentage of revenue, yes, EDA has always had the need

insights.claim: The Synopsys CEO says pace is his biggest worry, since transforming an engineering workforce to a new workflow while still delivering current customer commitments is very hard even though easy on a slide.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Execution and workflow-adoption risk may slow realized benefits of AI-driven design at established chip companies.
insights.quote: The pace, the pace, the pace.
insights.locator: Given all this change, what worries you?

insights.claim: Interface IP that connects chip-to-chip and chip-to-system is increasingly customized by hyperscalers, because general-purpose IP leaves area and performance unoptimized and loses competitiveness.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Custom interface IP is a growing, sticky revenue pool tied to hyperscaler silicon programs.
insights.locator: There is what I describe as the classic EDA products

insights.claim: As AI moves from digital to physical products such as vehicles and robots, designers must model the electronics, the mechanical system and the operating environment together, and Synopsys positions its Ansys acquisition as providing multiphysics sign-off to avoid overdesign.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Silicon-to-system simulation is the strategic rationale for the Ansys deal and a growth vector beyond chips.
insights.locator: As AI expands from digital to physical

insights.claim: A system is defined at multiple abstraction levels, since an advanced package is a system but becomes a component of a rack, subsystem or data center, which complicates co-design.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Co-analysis across abstraction layers is the tooling gap that creates demand for integrated multiphysics platforms.
insights.locator: The hardest part for me to describe

insights.claim: Digital twins of individual domains, such as a car's electronics or crash testing, are used by customers today, but a broadly used twin spanning electronics, physics and the operating environment does not yet exist.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: A complete system-level digital twin remains an unmet need and potential product opportunity for simulation vendors.
insights.quote: is there a digital twin that encompasses the electronics, the physics, the environment in which that system operates, that today is available and broadly used by customers? Not really.
insights.locator: The concept of digital twin or virtualization

insights.claim: Synopsys's CEO says building sophisticated intelligent systems without a digital twin would take forever at astronomical cost.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Digital twins are positioned as necessary infrastructure for complex systems, supporting long-run simulation demand.
insights.quote: I'm not sure how you can build a future sophisticated intelligent system without having a digital twin.
insights.locator: Today customers are using it

insights.claim: Chinese robotics and EV companies founded two or three years ago with a fully digital design approach have taped out silicon, put it in a car and run software within weeks, and update the whole car every nine months to a year versus four to six years for traditional OEMs.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Digital-first Chinese entrants run much faster product cycles than incumbent automakers, a competitive threat and an EDA demand driver.
insights.locator: The one place I'm always amazed at

insights.claim: 3D-ICs are already sitting in data centers, but running intense workloads creates thermal issues inside the package that cause some chiplets to warp or crack, making it a mechanical rather than electronic challenge.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Thermo-mechanical reliability is a real yield and field-failure risk for advanced packaging in AI data centers.
insights.quote: It's causing some of the chiplets to warp or to crack.
insights.locator: Yes. There are many chips sitting in data centers today that are 3D-ICs

insights.claim: Bringing physics simulation early into 3D-IC architecture, together with the workload, was the key thesis for Synopsys acquiring Ansys, because the future is heterogeneous integration of multiple chips.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Physics-aware design raises tool content per advanced-package design and supports the Ansys deal rationale.
insights.locator: That was actually the key thesis for Synopsys to acquire Ansys

insights.claim: Designing the multi-die package in the context of the actual workload is essential because field surprises come from overlooked corner cases where a system overheats and breaks.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Workload-aware thermal analysis reduces field failures and is a selling point for system-level EDA.
insights.locator: Yes, actually, this is where I mentioned the workload
